Looking at this problem, I need to determine whether some poset can have quasiwidth > width.

**Definitions.** The *width* w(P) of a poset P is the maximum size of an antichain (a set of pairwise incomparable elements). A *quasi-antichain* is a subset of P that contains no chain of three elements (equivalently, the induced subposet has height at most 2). The *quasiwidth* qw(P) is the maximum size of a quasi-antichain.

Note that every antichain is automatically a quasi-antichain (it has no chain of size 2, hence none of size 3), so qw(P) ≥ w(P) always. The question is whether this inequality can be **strict**.

**Construction.** Let P = {a, b, c} be the 3-element chain with a < b < c.

**Width.** Every pair of elements in P is comparable, so the only antichains are singletons. Thus:
$$w(P) = 1.$$

**Quasiwidth.** The subset {a, b} contains the chain a < b (of size 2) but no chain of size 3, so it is a quasi-antichain of size 2. Hence qw(P) ≥ 2. On the other hand, the only subset of size 3 is P itself, which contains the 3-element chain a < b < c, so P is **not** a quasi-antichain. Therefore:
$$qw(P) = 2.$$

**Conclusion.** We have qw(P) = 2 > 1 = w(P). Thus, yes, there exists a poset whose quasiwidth strictly exceeds its width. ∎

**Remark.** More generally, for any height-2 poset P (e.g., n minimal elements below n maximal elements, all comparable across levels), the entire ground set is a quasi-antichain, giving qw(P) = |P|, while w(P) equals the size of the largest level — so the ratio qw/w can be made arbitrarily close to 2. The 3-element chain is the minimal witness.
